title: How To Give A Warning That Curbs Misbehavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/01/04/how-to-give-a-warning-that-curbs-misbehavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin reframes the classroom warning as a courtesy rather than a threat—an acknowledgment that a rule was broken, without any accompanying anger or lecture. He offers three guidelines for delivering warnings effectively: staying calm, being clear about which rule was broken, and being unfailingly consistent, both in tone and in following through with time-out when warnings are ignored. He contrasts this approach with the common mistake of delivering warnings with intimidation or a glare, which breeds resentment rather than compliance. The piece closes by urging teachers to explicitly teach students that a warning is not a sign of trouble but a second-chance 'statement of grace.'
points: A properly delivered warning is a courtesy—an acknowledgment that a rule was broken, not a threat or display of anger.
Warnings should be delivered calmly, from a noticeable distance, without waiting for a response before walking away.
Clarity about which specific rule was broken helps students place responsibility on themselves rather than on the teacher.
A warning only retains its power if it's consistently backed up by the next step (time-out) when ignored.
Teachers should explicitly teach students that receiving a warning does not mean they are 'in trouble,' framing it as a second chance.
quotes: It’s a declaration of free grace you offer by letting them know that you are aware a rule has been broken.
Their warning is more of a threat than a courtesy. It’s the heavy hand of the law meted out with a glare and an air of intimidation.
Remember, you’re providing a service. What they do with the information is up to them.
A warning from you is like a red light that pops up on the dashboard of your car.
Done right, a warning is a statement of grace that acknowledges that we all make mistakes.
